about: NOMAD lab book: one entry per experiment, newest last. Numbers in {curly braces} are filled from our result files by src/book/build_book.py, so they always match the latest run. Add an entry after every experiment.

experiments.title: Collecting the law into one rulebook
experiments.question: Can we get every rule that decides whether a Barcelona shop may become a home into one searchable file, with the exact article each rule comes from?
did: Downloaded national laws from the BOE open-data API, the 5 main parts of the Spanish building code (CTE) as PDFs, the Catalan laws from the Portal Jurídic, and the Barcelona and metropolitan plan rules (PGM, OME).
Cut every text into pieces (an article, a table, a paragraph) and kept the law, the article number and the web address with each piece.
Scanned PDFs were read with Tesseract OCR (Catalan + Spanish), column by column.
experiments.result: {rulebook_pieces} pieces from {norms} norms at 4 levels (Spain, Catalonia, metropolitan area, Barcelona).
learned: The CTE PDFs use a special font for ≥ and ≤; without a fix every limit lost its sign.
An early clean-up deleted short words like "no", which flipped the meaning of a rule. Clean-up now never deletes letters or digits.
Some sites (gencat, amb.cat) block scripts; those PDFs were downloaded by hand in the browser.
experiments.decision: One file, data/rulebook.jsonl, is the only source of legal text for every later stage.
figures: Pieces of law per norm, coloured by level. The building code's health part (CTE-DB-HS) and Catalonia's planning law (TRLU) are the biggest.

experiments.title: Testing 9 rules on real flats
experiments.question: If we write the main housing rules as code, how many real, already-built flats pass them? This tells us whether our rules are read correctly.
did: Wrote 9 rules from Decret 141/2012 (Catalan housing quality) and the Barcelona plan, each with its article.
Ran them on {flats_tested} real Swiss flats (Swiss Dwellings v3.0.0) and {resplan_tested} plans from ResPlan.
Ran the shell rules on {shops_tested} Swiss commercial units (shops).
experiments.result: {flats_all_pass} of Swiss flats and {resplan_all_pass} of ResPlan plans pass every rule. {shops_convertible} of {shops_tested} shops pass the rules an empty shell can meet.
learned: Swiss flats are not built for Catalan rules, so most failures are expected. The useful part is which rule fails.
The façade rule (MPGM 2004 DA1 2.b) fails most often. Bigger flats pass more often.
Swiss window heights are measured from the building's base, not the room floor; this had to be corrected.
experiments.decision: The rules work on real data; the generator must pass all 9 before a plan is shown as "works".
figures: Share of plans passing each rule. Shops are tested only on the rules a bare shell can meet.
Swiss flats: the more bedrooms, the more often all rules pass.

experiments.title: Cleaning the shop dataset
experiments.question: Which of the real shops are worth trying to convert at all?
did: Removed shops that can never be a home under the rules: too small, too low, or without enough façade with windows.
experiments.result: {clean_shops} of {shops_tested} shops kept.
learned: Size is the main reason: most dropped shops are under 40 m² (Barcelona minimum).
experiments.decision: The generator and every later test use these {clean_shops} shops (data/clean/nomad_shells.json).
figures: Why shops were dropped. Green = kept.

experiments.title: Learning room sizes from flats that pass
experiments.question: How big should each room be? We do not want to invent sizes.
did: Took only the Swiss flats that pass all 9 rules and measured their rooms, by flat type.
experiments.result: Typical (median) and compact (25th percentile) sizes for studio, 1-, 2- and 3-bedroom flats.
learned: A typical 1-bed that passes is about 58 m² useful; a studio about 49 m².
experiments.decision: The generator uses these learned sizes; "compact rooms" in Grasshopper switches to the smaller set.
figures: Room sizes learned per flat type (typical = median).

experiments.title: First plan generator: flats along the façade
experiments.question: Given a shop's outline and façade, can the computer place the flats asked for (for example 2 × 1-bed + 1 × 2-bed) so that every flat passes every rule?
did: Living rooms and bedrooms go in a front band along the façade (daylight); kitchen, bath and hall in a band behind.
Every placed flat is checked against the 9 rules, each failure named with its article.
Asked 6 unit mixes of all {clean_shops} shops, with typical and compact room sizes.
experiments.result: With "as many flats as fit", {shops_with_proposal} of {clean_shops} shops get a working proposal, {flats_generated} flats in total.
learned: Bigger mixes run out of façade: 2 × 1-bed + 1 × 2-bed works in about 1 shop in 5.
The deep inside of a shop stays empty (see the 3D view): no light reaches it without a patio.
Only façades that already have windows are used.
experiments.decision: Stage 6 v2 must add patios (PGM art. 225.7), back flats and a shared corridor.
figures: Share of shops where every flat asked for fits and passes.
Generated plans, top view. Grey = shop, coloured = rooms, red = fails a rule, blue line = façade.
The same idea in 3D: flats line the street façade; the deep interior is unused.

experiments.title: Reading a plan drawing
experiments.question: Can NOMAD take a plan image or PDF and find the shop's outline, area and street façade by itself?
did: Used the floorplan-to-3d AI model (MIT, from a team link) to label walls, doors and windows; dark lines also count as walls.
Straighten the plan, fill in from the paper's edge, close door and shopfront gaps, keep the inside as one outline.
Drew all 180 shops as test plans with known answers, plus messy copies with text, dimensions, furniture and scan noise.
experiments.result: With one known size given: outline overlap {reader_iou_given} (1 = perfect), area within 10% on {reader_area10_given} of plans. Without a size the reader's own scale guess is {reader_scale_err} off.
learned: The model labels windows as doors, so both now count as façade openings.
Wide glass shopfronts let the fill leak inside; fixed by closing straight gaps along a wall line.
Guessing the scale is unreliable, so NOMAD always asks for one dimension (known_facade_m).
experiments.decision: Reader v1 is in NOMAD.gh: Plan file + known_facade_m + read plan.
figures: A test plan, its messy copy, and what the reader found: red = outline, green = façade.
Accuracy over 180 plans. Blue = one size given; ochre = scale guessed.
First test on downloaded plan images: the model's wall and door pixels.

experiments.title: GitHub scan and a plan-reader race
experiments.question: Has someone already built (and shared) the parts we need: reading a plan, flags, better plans, 3D? If so, use their code.
did: Searched GitHub for {repos_found} repos across stages 4–7 and checked each one's licence, last update and fit (docs/github_repos.csv).
Downloaded MitUNet (2026, a sharper wall model) and raced 4 wall readers on 60 clean and 60 messy test plans, one size given.
experiments.result: On messy plans: ours {race_f3d_messy} area within 10%, MitUNet {race_mitunet_messy}, dark lines alone {race_dark_messy}, AI model alone {race_f3d_only_messy}.
learned: MitUNet did not help on our drawings; plain dark lines are as good, because our test plans draw walls solid black.
Most strong plan models (Raster2Seq, MitUNet, CubiCasa) have non-commercial weights (CC BY-NC): fine for the master, not for a product.

No repo checks Catalan or Barcelona rules; the closest re-usable parts are IfcOpenShell/IfcTester (rules on BIM), shapely (exact circle test), OR-Tools CP-SAT and the Autodesk floorplate generator (unit mix + corridor), and IfcOpenShell + trimesh for 3D.
experiments.decision: Keep our reader. Next tests need real scanned plans (CubiCasa5K) where AI should matter. Stage 5–7 start from the repos marked Use / Copy the method.
figures: The race: blue = clean plans, ochre = messy plans.
The same messy plan read 4 ways. Red = outline, green = façade.

experiments.title: Flags on the plan, drawn in Rhino
experiments.question: Can NOMAD show on the plan itself which parts are usable for housing, which rules pass or fail, and give one clear answer: YES, PARTLY or NO?
did: Wrote the Stage 5 check (src/check/flags.py): one rule card per rule with OK/FAIL, the value, and the article it comes from; a new check that every flat stays inside the shop; and the verdict.
Drew it as a sheet in Rhino from NOMAD.gh: the plan tinted by daylight from the façade, flats and rooms labelled, rule cards (leaders only where a rule fails), 'How it was checked' and 'Result'.
Added 'make sheet' and 'run inbox' to NOMAD.gh: drop plans in nomad/inbox and each one gets a sheet (PNG + numbers).
Ran the check on all {clean_shops} shops for three unit mixes.
experiments.result: Asking 2 × 1-bed + 1 × 2-bed: {s5_yes} shops YES, {s5_partly} PARTLY, {s5_no} NO. The card that fails most is 'Flats that fit' ({s5_fit_fail} shops): the shop runs out of façade or depth. {s5_dark20} shops have more than 20% of their floor dark.
learned: Almost no flat that fits breaks a housing rule; the problem is space along the façade. That is Stage 6's job (patios, back flats, corridor).
The new 'inside the shop' check caught a generator flat that crossed the outline on a read plan.
Taken from GitHub for this step: nothing. The rule checks already existed in our code; IfcOpenShell/IfcTester checks BIM models and is kept for Stage 7.
Rhino stopped obeying /runscript at start-up after a plug-in update; a helper now types the command into a fresh Rhino (src/rhino/run_in_rhino.ps1).
experiments.decision: Stage 5 v1 lives in NOMAD.gh. The daylight part stays as it is (Bars owns the daylight analysis). Next: Stage 6, better plans.
figures: Four shops checked as they are. The verdict is written under each plan; the light colours show daylight from the façade (blue line).

experiments.title: Before and after: the smallest change that houses more flats
experiments.question: When the flats asked for do not fit, which is the smallest building change that makes more of them fit and pass every rule?
did: Wrote Stage 6 (src/generate/better.py): try the shop as it is; then cut a light patio into the dark interior, add a 1,20 m shared corridor from the street, and line the patio with back flats. One patio at a time, kept only if it houses more passing flats; ties go to the fewest and smallest patios.

Rules from our rulebook: patio = Decret 141/2012 Annex 1 2.5.1 (fits a 3 m circle, at least 9 m²); corridor = CTE DB-SUA Anejo A (accessible route at least 1,20 m). A cross patio runs across narrow deep shops, with an open gallery behind it so every back flat has a door.
Redrew the sheets the way you asked: white, no grid, no boxes, clear Arial text, before and after side by side, the verdict large and translucent over each plan.

Every sheet is saved as an experiment that NOMAD.gh draws into rhino/NOMAD.3dm (layer 06 NOMAD experiments), so they all stay in the one Rhino file. Tested on a copy of the file: 7 experiments, 726 objects.
experiments.result: Asking 2 × 1-bed + 1 × 2-bed of all {clean_shops} shops: shops where everything works {s6_works_v1} → {s6_works_after}; flats that pass {s6_flats_v1} → {s6_flats_after}. Asking 5 × 1-bed + 2 × 2-bed: flats that pass {s6_flats_v1_big} → {s6_flats_after_big}.
learned: The gain is real but small. What stops most shops is the length of street façade, not daylight depth: only 21 of 180 shops are deep enough (about 18 m) for a patio plus back flats.
Narrow deep shops (about 7 m wide, like the warehouse in Fig. E09.2) cannot hold a corridor and a back flat side by side: the answer stays NO, and the sheet says why.
Placing small flats first sometimes fits more than big flats first; the generator now tries both (no building work).
Taken from GitHub: nothing. The Autodesk floorplate generator's corridor idea matched ours; writing it in our own generator was less work than porting TypeScript.
experiments.decision: Stage 6 v2 is in NOMAD.gh (the 3D shows the after plan; patios light blue, corridor grey). Next: new windows in blind street walls (needs cadastre data on which walls face the street) and Stage 7, the 3D model.
figures: A deep warehouse: before, 1 of 3 flats; after a cross patio + shared corridor, 2 of 3. Drawn by NOMAD in Rhino.
A 7 m wide warehouse with 2,7 m of façade: no patio layout fits, so the answer stays NO.
A plan drawing read by NOMAD: the second 1-bed does not fit and no building work helps.
A shop where all 3 flats already fit and pass: no change needed.
All 180 shops: flats that pass every rule, first generator vs Stage 6.

experiments.title: The demo: from a commercial plan to homes, in Rhino
experiments.question: Using only the rules we collected, can NOMAD take a commercial floor plan, say YES / PARTLY / NO, draw three 2D layouts with the number of homes, and build a 3D model of each?
did: Stage 4: a plan drawing is read (outline + façade) - or a shop comes from the dataset.
Stage 5: flags on the shop as it is, for the flats asked for (2 × 1-bed + 1 × 2-bed): every rule with its article, and the verdict.

Stage 6: three 2D iterations - 1 as asked, 2 as asked with compact (still legal) rooms, 3 as many homes as fit - each may add a light patio and a 1,20 m shared corridor when that houses more flats; each is checked again.
Stage 7: a 3D model of each iteration, built in Rhino under its plan (walls cut at 1,20 m so the rooms show).
Five shops (one read from a drawing) drawn by NOMAD.gh in Rhino; every one is kept in rhino/NOMAD.3dm on layer 06 NOMAD experiments. Then all 180 shops for the totals.
experiments.result: All {clean_shops} shops, asked 2 × 1-bed + 1 × 2-bed. Stage 5 as it is: {it_flag_yes} YES, {it_flag_partly} PARTLY, {it_flag_no} NO. Homes: iteration 1 {it1_homes}, iteration 2 {it2_homes}, iteration 3 {it3_homes} (YES in {it3_yes} shops; at least one home in {it3_any} shops).
learned: Compact rooms (still legal) add about one home in seven; asking for 'as many as fit' instead of a fixed mix adds the most.
About 30 shops cannot hold even one home: too small, too narrow, or too little façade.

The audit found and fixed: stale plan readings, a memory leak in Rhino, pictures not embedded in the 3dm, experiments that could drift from their pictures, a silent scale guess and the wall band covering complex plans (docs/audit_2026-10-28.md).
experiments.decision: This is what we show. Next: new windows in blind walls (cadastre data), Bars's daylight analysis, and IFC / glTF export of the Stage 7 models.
figures: A plan drawing read by NOMAD: flags, three iterations, and their 3D models.
A shop that already works (YES): iteration 3 fits one more home.
A deep warehouse: a cross patio and a shared corridor add a back flat.
A large shop: 7 homes as asked, 12 when as many as fit.
A 7 m wide warehouse: NO in every iteration, and the rules say why.

experiments.title: From zoning to walls: doors and windows in Rhino
experiments.question: Can the Stage 7.1 zoning (each room a coloured block) be turned into a real model with walls, doors and windows, so the rooms and halls read as spaces?
did: Same layouts as Stage 6 and the same E05 colours: each room floor in its colour (red if it fails a rule), patios light blue, the shared corridor grey.
Walls 2,70 m high with no roof: the shell 30 cm, partitions 10 cm, placed in the 20 cm gap NOMAD leaves between rooms so two neighbours make one wall.
Windows in the street facade, 60% of each room's width and 1,5 m tall (sill 0,90 m), as light-blue glass: the same window the Stage 5 check assumes (Decret 141/2012 Annex 1 3.9.1, 1/8 of the floor).
A door of 0,80 m from every room to its flat's hall (or living room), and an entry door of 0,90 m in the street facade for each flat (flats are entered from the street).
Drawn by NOMAD.gh under each zoning model (layer 06 NOMAD experiments::<shop>::walls iteration k) and captured from above in Rhino.
experiments.result: All five demo shops built: for the large shop, iteration 3 has 12 homes, 32 windows, 12 entries; every layout shows its rooms, halls and openings.
learned: Blocks are best for reading the zoning (which room is which); walls are best for reading the space (how you walk in, where the light comes from). We keep both, one after the other.
A steep view is needed: from low down the walls hide the coloured floors.
Door positions are a design assumption (centre of the shared wall), not a rule check.
experiments.decision: Stage 7 is now two steps: 7.1 zoning, 7.2 walls, doors, windows. Next: check door widths and the hall turning circle against the rules, then IFC export.
figures: A plan drawing: the zoning, then walls, doors and windows.
A shop that works: four homes along the street, each with its entry and windows.
A deep warehouse: two flats around a light patio.

experiments.title: Zoning: can each empty shop in Barcelona become housing at all?
experiments.question: Before any plan is drawn: does the urban zoning of each empty ground-floor premises in Barcelona admit housing?
did: Took the 6,149 empty premises (for rent, for sale or both) of the Ajuntament's 2024 ground-floor census (Open Data BCN, CC BY 4.0).
Downloaded the 12,583 zoning polygons of Barcelona from the Mapa Urbanístic de Catalunya (MUC, Departament de Territori), once, 2,000 per request.

Matched every premises to the zone it stands in (point in polygon, EPSG:25831). The census point is the shop door: 60 doors fell in the street polygon and take the zone of the building behind (nearest non-street zone within 8 m).

Answered each zone with PGM art. 225.7 (MPGM 1999): housing on the ground floor is admitted in the zones built along street lines (12, 13a, 13b, 14b, 15); industrial zones and systems (streets, parks, facilities) are not; specific volumetry, isolated buildings and 22@ depend on their own plan.
experiments.result: 5,026 of 6,149 empty premises (82 %) stand in a zone that admits housing on the ground floor (13a 2,334, 12 1,383, 13b 1,259, 15 49); 817 depend on their zone's own plan; 306 do not (facilities, parks, industry, port). In the Eixample: 1,160 of 1,224 (95 %).
learned: Zoning is rarely the problem in the dense city: four in five empty shops pass the first gate. The rules inside the shop (façade, light, size) decide.
The 'check' group is not random: specific volumetry (635) and 22@ (58) need the detailed plan, which the MUC does not carry.
Art. 225.7 adds a condition NOMAD does not check yet: a room facing the inner block needs that part unbuilt, at least 6 m deep and 4,5 m wide.
experiments.decision: Zoning is NOMAD's first gate (step 3, now running). Next: the inner-block condition of art. 225.7, and the 817 'check' premises against their detailed plans.
figures: Every empty ground-floor premises in Barcelona, by what its zone allows (MUC, Generalitat; census 2024, Ajuntament).

experiments.title: Rule cards and a golden set: does NOMAD use the right numbers?
experiments.question: Does every number NOMAD checks match the official text, with the right article, and does it check every rule it should?
did: Wrote 16 rule cards (rules/rules.json), each quoting its sentence of the official text from the rulebook. Two automatic checks: the quote is word for word in the official text, and the number is in the quote. 15 pass; the CTE corridor card goes to review (the PDF table was garbled).
Wrote a golden set of 16 questions (eval/golden_set.csv): 10 from the team's gold cards (Exp 2) and 6 from the text, every answer found word for word in its source.
Scored NOMAD's code against it: the value each check uses and the article it cites. Also scored plain keyword search (BM25) of the rulebook: does the right article come first?
Fixed what the evaluation found, and scored again.
experiments.result: Before the fixes: 12 of 16 right (3 rules not checked; 2,50 m used where a shop conversion needs 2,40 m; one article wrong). After: 16 of 16, every citation right. Keyword search finds the right article first for 13 of 16 questions and in the top 5 for 15.
learned: The golden set found a real bug: 8 shops of 2,44-2,45 m had been thrown out. As a change of use (Decret 141/2012 Annex 4 group C) they only need 2,40 m: the dataset grows from 180 to 188 shops.
The living-dining-kitchen minimum of 20 m² (Annex 1 3.7.1, in the team's gold cards) is marked 'No vigent' in the consolidated text: it no longer applies.
Annex 4 group C also exempts Annex 1 section 2 for a shop conversion, so the patio size rule is stricter than needed (safe).
experiments.decision: Three checks added (living room on the façade >= 2,20 m, wet rooms >= 2,20 m high, hall >= 1 m), 2,40 m for conversions, art. 323 cited for zone 13. Re-score the golden set after every rule change.

experiments.title: The 3D as IFC and glTF: the model leaves Rhino
experiments.question: Can every layout's walls model be opened outside Rhino, in BIM software and on the web?
did: Ran the Rhino walls code (Stage 7.2) outside Rhino and recorded each solid: walls, glass, doors, room floors, slab.
Wrote IFC 4 with IfcOpenShell (LGPL): IfcWall, IfcWindow, IfcDoor, IfcSlab, and an IfcSpace per room with its name, flat and floor area.
Wrote glTF (.glb) with trimesh (MIT): one mesh per colour, glass see-through.
experiments.result: 12 IFC + 12 glTF files for the demo shops (results/model3d/); the IFC files pass IfcOpenShell's schema check with 0 problems. The largest: 497 walls, 26 windows, 48 doors, 60 rooms.
learned: One geometry, three outputs: Rhino, IFC and glTF cannot drift apart.
The export found 6 window slivers on very short façade edges; they are now dropped in Rhino too.
experiments.decision: Stage 7 is complete. Next: open the IFC in a BIM viewer with the team, and the glTF in a web page.

experiments.title: The plan reader on 398 real scanned plans
experiments.question: Our plan reader scored 0.93 on plans we drew ourselves. How does it do on real scanned floor plans it has never seen?
did: Took the CubiCasa5K test split: 400 real Finnish plan scans (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) that our wall model was never trained or tuned on (checked: 0 overlap with its train and validation lists).

Built each answer from the plan's SVG: the indoor rooms and the walls between them, without balconies, terraces or garages, shrunk by one wall thickness (the first version split thick log walls into pieces, and was redone).
Raced four wall readers with one known size: ours (AI model + dark lines), dark lines only, the AI model only, and MitUNet from GitHub.
experiments.result: On 398 real scans: dark lines only 0.71 median overlap (26 % of areas within 10 %); ours 0.69 (20 %); MitUNet 0.68 (19 %); the AI model alone 0.61 (19 %). On our own drawings the same reader scored 0.93 (77 %).
learned: Real scans are much harder: coloured walls, open plans, text and dimension lines, and several floors on one sheet.
On real scans the AI wall models do not help yet: plain dark lines do best. Both AI models were trained on clean drawings of the same plans, not on scans.
A wrong answer key can look like a bad reader: the first answers were too small, and fixing them changed the scores.
experiments.decision: Keep asking for one size and showing what was found so the user can correct it. Next: fine-tune the wall model on scans (CubiCasa's train split), and test on CVC-FP (122 scans from the UAB, Barcelona).

experiments.title: NOMAD on Barcelona's real empty shops
experiments.question: Does the whole pipeline work on real Barcelona buildings, not only test plans?
did: Matched the 6,149 empty ground-floor premises of the 2024 census to Catastro INSPIRE buildings, built each shop's shell (street façade = edge facing a street polygon in the MUC), cleaned the errors, and ran NOMAD's check and three layouts on every shop that is alone on its ground floor.
experiments.result: 5,688 of 6,056 premises kept after cleaning; NOMAD ran on 1,694. As they are: 155 YES, 946 PARTLY, 593 NO; after the smallest change 225 YES. Up to 2,855 homes fit, in 1,192 shops.
learned: Most real shops share their ground floor with other premises: the Catastro outline is then the whole floor, so those 3,680 are labelled and left out until the CAT file splits them.
The street façade, not the area, is what limits the homes.
experiments.decision: Real shops are now the main test set. Next: the Catastro CAT file (src/building/cat_file.py, ready) to cut shared floors into each shop.
figures: Real shop shells from the Catastro: outline, and street façade in blue.

experiments.title: The website: owner mode, plan upload, three languages, report
experiments.question: Can an owner use NOMAD alone, without Rhino?
did: Website with NOMAD's own Python running in the browser (Pyodide): check an address, design homes with your flat mix and sizes, 3D of each layout, the city in 3D.

Added a simple view in plain words, Catalan and Spanish, upload of a plan drawing (outline traced from dark walls, or clicked by hand when the drawing is a scan), a value estimate from idealista18 asking prices, saved shops side by side, and a PDF report.
experiments.result: The same answer as Rhino in about 12 s in the browser. Plan upload traces clean drawings; on a scanned plan the tracer fails and the click-the-corners mode is needed.
learned: An outline from a scan needs the AI wall model, not dark lines: that is why the plan reader is being fine-tuned on real scans.
experiments.decision: Publish; the uploaded-plan reader moves to the fine-tuned model when it beats dark lines.
figures: Page 1 of a NOMAD PDF report: the shop as it is and three layouts.

experiments.title: Fine-tuning the plan reader on real scans
experiments.question: Does training the floorplan-to-3d model on real CubiCasa5K scans make it read real scanned plans better?
did: Fetched 182 training and 40 check scans from the CubiCasa5K train/val splits (never the test split), read straight from the Zenodo zip.
Trained the published weights for 8 rounds on the laptop GPU (RTX 3060, about 2 minutes).
Graded it on the same 398 real test scans as before, with one known size.
experiments.result: On the 40 check scans the wall overlap rose from 0.098 to 0.118. On the 398 test scans it got worse: outline overlap 0.617 (published model 0.685, dark lines 0.709), area within 10 % on 11 % (published 20 %, dark lines 26 %).
learned: 182 scans and 8 rounds are not enough: the model learned the new scans' walls a little and forgot part of what it did well.
Dark pixels are still the best wall reader on scans.
experiments.decision: Keep the published weights. A real fine-tune needs the full train split (about 4,000 scans) and a longer run; the download is the bottleneck (about 1-2 scans a minute).

experiments.title: The rulebook as one book: the original official PDFs
experiments.question: Can a layman reach every regulation, and see which ones decided their project?
did: Compiled the 23 official PDFs (BOE consolidated laws, the five CTE documents, Catalan decree, laws and circulars, PGM changes, metropolitan ordinances, the Ajuntament guide) into one book, pages unchanged.

Added a cover, a plain-language page on how to read it, a clickable index with one plain line per document, a divider per level, a page number on every page, PDF bookmarks, and an invisible OCR layer on the scanned PGM pages.
Found the page (and the paragraph) of each of the 17 rules NOMAD checks; the website's flipbook bookmarks and highlights them for each project.
experiments.result: 1,408 pages, 54 MB (the 117 MB B1600 scan re-encoded to greyscale). Online: 26 files under 11 MB each. All 17 rules located; 13 with highlighted paragraphs (the 4 on scanned pages open at the right page).
learned: The habitability numbers for a shop conversion sit on 10 pages of one decree (Decret 141/2012, Annex 1 and 4): the bookmarks make that visible.
Scanned plan documents can be searched once the OCR text is added as an invisible layer.
experiments.decision: The flipbook is the rulebook's public face; the search viewer stays for the team.

experiments.title: Bars's daylight model on Barcelona's real empty shops
experiments.question: How much daylight do the real empty shops get, and how deep is the liveable part?
did: Took Bars's Experiment 1 unchanged (iaac-maai/nomad: 50 Ladybug/Honeybee daylight simulations, XGBoost, his features and assumptions).
Measured each of NOMAD's real shop shells: depth from the street façade, façade width, distance and height of the building across the street (a ray into the Catastro buildings).
Trained his second target too (share of floor with daylight factor >= 2 %) to get the lit depth: how far from the window the floor stays at DF >= 2 %.
experiments.result: 1,650 shops: median predicted daylight factor 1.2 %; 420 well lit (>= 2 %), 858 some daylight, 372 dark (< 1 %). Median lit depth 2.95 m (our fixed assumption was 5.5 m). On the 111 shops Bars also modelled, geometry agrees within centimetres and the predicted DF median 1.15 % vs his 1.12 %. Only 211 shops are fully inside his training ranges.
learned: Most ground floors are darker than the 5.5 m light band assumed: daylight, not the rules, limits liveable depth.
Daylight is not a legal threshold in Decret 141/2012 (that is window area >= 1/8), so it is used as a liveability signal, not a fail.
experiments.decision: Show Bars's prediction with every real shop (map card, Design homes, Grasshopper component 7) and use DF < 1 % as 'not liveable' in the avoid answer. More simulations at wider ranges would make it firmer.

experiments.title: 'Avoid' as an answer: which shops should not become homes
experiments.question: Can NOMAD tell a city where NOT to convert?
did: Gave each of the 6,149 empty premises the first answer that applies: not allowed (zone), not liveable (no home fits, or dark by Bars's model), keep it a shop (retail within 100 m in the city's lowest 10 %, a NOMAD design choice), candidate, or not modelled.
Shops nearby counted from the 61,875 active premises of the 2024 census.
experiments.result: 896 candidates, 714 not liveable, 565 keep it a shop (4 or fewer shops within 100 m; city median 16), 306 not allowed, 3,668 not modelled yet (mostly shared ground floors).
learned: Madrid's Plan RESIDE protects shops on commercial streets: the 'keep it a shop' idea already exists in city policy.
experiments.decision: New map mode on the website: 'NOMAD's answer, with avoid'. The 10 % cut is a design choice to discuss with the team.

experiments.title: NOMAD.gh split into small components
experiments.question: Can the Grasshopper file be read and reused step by step (review: 'a node with 15 inputs is not usable')?
did: Rebuilt NOMAD.gh as 10 components (read plan, shop, zoning, flats asked, flat sizes, check + layouts, daylight, 3D preview, make, this file), each with at most 6 inputs; objects pass between them in a wrapper.
Verified in Rhino with a Barcelona address (Valencia 640).
experiments.result: 10 components, 0 errors; the report shows zoning, Bars's daylight (DF 3.3 %), the before / after verdict and every rule card.
learned: Grasshopper splits a Python dict into its keys on a wire: whole objects must travel wrapped.
experiments.decision: The old single component stays in grasshopper/archive.

experiments.title: Iterations as circulation strategies (Finch-style)
experiments.question: Can the 2D iterations be real design options, each a different way to reach the flats, as Finch builds its floor-plate options?
did: Studied Finch 3D: options are circulation strategies (existing circulation, new cores, corridor + core), searched over parameters and scored with weight sliders.

Rebuilt the iterations in src/generate/plan2.py as strategies: flats on both façades (back to back, half the depth each), a 1.20 m corridor to the block-interior façade, and small flats filling every reachable façade. Each is searched over corridor width, position and flat order, and scored with one set of weights.
A strategy is shown only if it changes the plan; if none adds a home, 'street flats only' is shown with the reason.
Back flats more than 25 m from the street door are dropped (CTE DB-SI SI 3); proposals show only flats that pass.
Compared old and new generators on 300 real Barcelona shops and 188 test shops.
experiments.result: Real shops: most homes 497 -> 379, homes as asked 333 -> 261, floor in homes 27 % -> 33 %. Test shops: 466 -> 421, 266 -> 248, 42 % -> 54 %. The old 'most homes' plans had 59 (real) and 19 (test) flats lit only by a patio.
learned: Decret 141/2012 Annex 1 3.6.1: a patio is not the flat's façade, and 3.6.2 asks façade >= S/9. That caps a flat's useful depth at about 9-10 m, so a through flat with a patio inside never passes (tested 5-13 m wide).
The real lever is more façade: a second façade facing the street, or the block interior within 25 m of the street door.
Fewer homes than before, but every home shown is legal and more of the floor is used.
experiments.decision: plan2 strategies replace the patio iterations in Rhino and on the website.
figures: Before: iterations from the old generator (patios, flats lit only by a patio).
After: as it is (left), then one iteration per circulation strategy.

experiments.title: What makes a flat habitable: 13,444 real plans measured
experiments.question: How do real, rule-passing flats use every square metre: entrance, circulation, light, room shapes, services? And where do NOMAD's plans differ?
did: Measured every room, door, window, entrance and fixture of the 13,444 Swiss Dwellings flats (0-3 bedrooms) that pass every NOMAD rule: 94,471 rooms (src/learn/habitability.py).
Built each flat's room graph from its doors and open connections, starting at the front door.
Measured NOMAD's own demo plans the same way.
experiments.result: Circulation 12 % of the flat, hall 1.75 m wide; front door into a hall (85 %) from a common stair or corridor; living and bedrooms on the façade (95 %); flats reach 6 m from the window. NOMAD's plans: circulation 16 %, hall 1.10 m, kitchen 1.6 m and 2nd bedroom 2.2 m wide, 34 % of the shop floor left unused, every flat entered from the street.
learned: Habitable means every room reached from the hall, no room walked through to reach a bedroom, living and bedrooms on the façade, baths and stores inside, and no scraps.
NOMAD's rooms pass the minimum law but are narrower than real rooms, and a third of the shop is wasted.
experiments.decision: Rebuild the flat layout on these rules (docs/habitability_rules.md) before anything else.
figures: How real flats split their useful floor, by type (median).
Clear width of each room type in real flats.
What each room is reached from: almost always the hall.

experiments.title: Real flats, stretched to fit: a plan library, a plan graph and door clearances (Finch's method)
experiments.question: Can NOMAD fill each flat with a real, architect-made plan instead of inventing the rooms, and still pass the law?
did: Squared the 13,444 rule-passing Swiss flats into a library of plan graphs: rooms as nodes, doors (with widths) and open connections as edges, the entrance, and which sides have windows (8,625 kept: every room rectilinear).

Added the law's door and turning rules: entrance and practicable-space doors >= 0,80 m, others >= 0,70 m, circulation >= 1 m, a 1,20 m circle in practicable spaces (Decret 141/2012 Annex 1 3.4), living room 2,80 m (3.7.2), kitchen 1,60 m (3.7.3); doors narrower than the law are widened.
Plan-graph checks: every room reached from the entrance hall, no bedroom only through another, a bathroom reached without crossing a bedroom, living room and bedrooms on a façade.

A stretch solver (as Finch's Cassowary): wall lines move as little as possible, walls locked, bathrooms and kitchens stiff, no room under its legal width; plans fit only between 80 % and 130 % of their own size and must fill their space (no dead corners).

New layout (src/generate/plan3.py): a street lobby and a shared hall behind the flats, flats along every façade the hall reaches within 25 m, through flats in pairs off a passage, side-entered flats off a passage for shallow shops.
experiments.result: 920 real flats NOMAD can use (51 studios, 290 one-beds, 454 two-beds, 125 three-beds); fits score 77-98. On 40 real Barcelona shops: 54 legal homes in 28 shops (old generator: 70 homes in 28 shops, with narrower invented rooms).
learned: Real one-sided flats are studios and 1-beds; real 2- and 3-beds have windows on two façades. A shop lit only from the street fits mostly small flats.
Real flats are entered from a hall behind them, not from the street: the shop needs a lobby and a shared hall, as a real building does.
What is left in a deep shop has no façade at all: it can only serve the building (storage, bike room).
experiments.decision: plan3 replaces plan2 in Rhino and on the website; the library is the source of every flat plan.
figures: The test shops: as it is, then the best layouts, every flat a real plan stretched to fit (diamond = flat entrance, squares = doors).
Real Barcelona shops: flats along the street and the side façades, off a shared hall from a street door.

experiments.title: The building's own stair, ResPlan, door swings, a plan gallery and weight sliders
experiments.question: What was NOMAD still missing from Finch's method (Grok's decoding): existing circulation, more real plans, door clearances, a ranked gallery, user weights?
did: Existing circulation: the Catastro's ground-floor common parts (portal, stair) added to 531 real shops (src/building/existing_core.py); no flat or hall is drawn over them, and the portal on the street becomes the flats' entrance.

ResPlan (17,000 plans, CC BY 4.0) squared into the library like the Swiss flats (6,920 kept); its net area does not match its drawn rooms, so each plan is scaled by its doors (median inner door = 0,80 m, an assumption).

Door swings: every door's leaf sweep (into the room from the hall, into the flat at the entrance); a 1,20 m circle clear of the sweeps in each practicable space (Decret 141/2012 Annex 1 3.4.1.e) and a 1,20 m circle in the hall in front of their doors (3.4.1.d).
Gallery: each flat keeps its three best real plans (identical flats counted once) with fit, stretch and room-by-room scores against real rooms; the website swaps them.
Weight sliders on the website (the flats asked, homes, floor used, plan fit), sent to the generator.
experiments.result: Street library: 761 real flats that pass every rule incl. door swings (575 Swiss Dwellings, 186 ResPlan; 390 two-beds). 40 real shops: 52 legal homes in 28 shops. Engine 1-2 s per shop in the browser.
learned: The door-swing rules are strict: a third of real Swiss plans fail the 1,20 m circle in the hall at the bathroom door - Catalan accessibility asks more than Swiss practice.
Weights mostly re-rank variants inside each way of reaching the flats; they change the plan little on most shops.
Large shops still waste façades the hall cannot reach within 25 m: next, a second street door and lobby.
experiments.decision: Keep the strict door rules (they are the law); add second lobbies for long façades next.
figures: Real shops: the building's own portal and stair (dark), door swings, flats along the street and the side façades.

experiments.title: A street door for every street façade, and the 25 m rule for every flat
experiments.question: Large shops left long street façades empty: can each get its own street door, lobby and hall?
did: Every street façade now gets street doors: one lobby per 40 m of façade, a shared hall behind its flats (src/generate/plan3.py: _street_block).
The 25 m rule (CTE DB-SI SI 3, one exit) is now checked for every flat, also the street flats: a flat whose door is further than 25 m from its street door along the hall is not placed.
experiments.result: 40 real shops: 53 legal homes in 28 shops; a 1,479 m² shop gets 8 homes off 4 street doors. The large demo shop drops from 8 to 6 homes: two of its earlier flats were more than 25 m from the street door.
learned: Fire escape distance, not the façade, limits how many flats one street door can serve.
experiments.decision: Keep: every flat within 25 m of a street door; one door per 40 m of street façade.
figures: Large shops: a street door and lobby on each street façade (lobbies in grey), every flat within 25 m of one.

experiments.title: Furniture, your own plans, generated plans and an assistant (the rest of the Finch list)
experiments.question: Can every flat be furnished as the law asks, can users add their own plans, what happens when no real plan fits, and can a chat assistant make bulk edits?
did: Furniture (src/generate/furnish.py): every flat gets what Decret 141/2012 Annex 1 asks for: a wardrobe 0,60 m deep, 1 m long over 6 m², 1,5 m over 8 m² (3.10.1); the bedroom square still free of door swings and the wardrobe (3.8); a worktop with sink and cooker and 1,00 m free in front (3.15.c, 3.7.3); WC, basin and shower (3.15.b, 3.11.1); a washing machine place (3.15.d); and the 1,20 m circle free of door swings and fixed equipment (3.4.1.e). Beds, sofa and dining table use typical sizes (an assumption, not law). Items are placed where they leave the biggest free square or circle. A practicable bathroom's door opens outward when that frees the circle.
Only flats that can be furnished stay in the library: 690 of the 761 real street flats. Every placed flat is furnished again after it is stretched.

Your own plans (src/library/own_plans.py): a DXF from Rhino or AutoCAD (rooms as closed polylines on layers named by use, in English, Catalan or Spanish; doors, windows, entrance and open connections as lines) or JSON. NOMAD squares it, builds its plan graph, checks and furnishes it like every real plan, and adds it to the library. On the website it is kept in the browser and used by the next layouts.

Generated plans: when no real plan fits a row, a real plan's room graph is re-proportioned beyond the usual 80-130 % (up to 65-160 %). It must pass every legal, graph and furniture check and is marked 'generated'. Graph2Plan / HouseDiffusion were not used: they need training data and a GPU, and their output would still have to pass these checks.

Ask NOMAD: a chat assistant on the website (like Finch's Archie). It runs on the viewer's own Claude account and can only change the request and weights, make the layouts, pick one, and swap plans in bulk (best fit, least stretched, largest, smallest).

Speed: a plan's gallery is built only for the kept layouts, and depth checks are cached. The large demo shop went from 16,8 s to 6,7 s in Python and from 19 s to 9 s in the browser, with the same homes.
experiments.result: 690 of 761 real street flats can be furnished as the law asks. 40 real shops: 58 legal homes in 28 shops, all furnished (57 without generated plans; generated plans add 1). 18 of 20 real flats drawn as DXF (rotated, in mm, Catalan layer names) are read back and pass; the other 2 have a back window and are rightly refused.
learned: The law's furniture rules (wardrobe, bedroom square, worktop, bathroom fittings, turning circle) reject 1 in 11 real flats. Furniture does not cost homes: the shops keep the same number.
Real plans fit almost every space NOMAD tries. Generated plans are a rare fallback, not a source of homes.
experiments.decision: Keep: every flat furnished and checked; own plans through DXF or JSON; generated plans only when no real plan fits, always marked; the assistant only acts through the page's own tools.
figures: Real flats furnished and checked. Thick outline: asked by law (wardrobe, worktop, WC, basin, shower, washing machine). Thin: typical sizes (bed, sofa, table). Red dashes: door swings.
Your own plan: a DXF drawn in Catalan layers, in mm and turned 23°, read by NOMAD, squared, checked and furnished.
A shop where no real plan fit the second row: the two 1-beds come from a re-proportioned real plan (marked generated) and pass every check.

experiments.title: No more red flats: the generator uses the final inside-the-shop test; smaller flats where the asked ones do not fit
experiments.question: Why did the website show red flats in layouts marked YES, and why do 12 of 40 real shops get no home?
did: Red flats: the generator allowed 3 % of a flat outside the shop, the Stage 5 check allowed none (every room corner inside within 15 cm). The generator now runs the same test (plan3._check 'inside'), so such a flat is never placed and the next one is tried.
The 'most homes' layouts also try 1-beds and studios at a spot where the asked flats do not fit (before, only once every asked flat was placed).
Shallow shops (under 6,5 m deep) also try 5 m deep flats (real street flats go down to 4,2 m).
experiments.result: 40 real shops: 57 legal homes in 28 shops, every one also passing the Stage 5 check (before: 58 counted, of which 6 crossed the outline and would have failed). 5 shops gain a home. The large demo shop: layouts with 2, 3 and 6 homes, no red flats. The 12 shops left empty have a street front under 6 m (or the deep part under 4 m wide), or are under 6 m deep: a 1,50 m lobby (CTE DB-SUA) plus the narrowest real flat (a 4,7 m studio; 4,44 m of façade for 40 m², Decret 141/2012 3.6.2) does not fit.
learned: The generator and the final check must use one test, or the count of homes is wrong.
Under 6 m of street front, a shop cannot take a home with its own legal entrance: it stays for other uses.
experiments.decision: Keep: one inside-the-shop test; fill with smaller flats where asked ones do not fit; shops under 6 m of front are reported as too narrow.
figures: Every flat inside the shop. Bottom: a shop that had no home now gets a studio off a shared hall.

experiments.title: Whole buildings: empty warehouses, commercial and office buildings
experiments.question: Can NOMAD also turn empty warehouses (naus) and commercial or office buildings into homes, not only ground-floor shops?
did: Candidates (src/zoning/warehouses.py): every Catastro building whose use is industrial, retail or office and holds no dwelling (4,823), with its PGM zone answer and a hint from the 2024 census of ground-floor premises (empty premises / no active business / active business). The census lists ground floors only, so this is a hint, not proof that a building is unused.

The law: a whole building is Decret 141/2012 Annex 4 Group B (total change of use). Annex 1 applies with patio surfaces -10 % and a 2,40 m clear height. Unlike a shop (Group C), the building rules of Annex 1 section 2 apply: accessible route (2.1), access and lift landing (2.2), stairs (2.3, CTE DB-SUA SUA 1 4.2), lift and second lift (2.4.1, 2.4.2, DB-SUA SUA 9 1.1.2), patios (2.5.1), community room (2.6).
Engine (src/generate/building.py):
- A warehouse with room for two 2,40 m storeys and a slab gets a mezzanine (two levels of homes). Commercial and office buildings keep their Catastro storeys (3,0 m each, an assumption).
- Deep floors get patios cut through them (3 m wide, Annex 1 2.5.1), with a 1,50 m passage across. A patio is kept only when the part behind it gets homes.
- Each part is laid out with real plans (plan3), and the same floor is stacked on every level.
- With more than one level, each street door becomes a core: two 1,00 m flights, a lift for a 1,00 x 1,25 m cabin, a 1,50 m landing, and room for the community room.

Website: a map layer 'Empty warehouses and commercial buildings', a building panel, and 'Design homes in this building' (clear height asked for warehouses). The plans show cores and patios; the 3D stacks the levels; the building rules appear as cards. Rhino: two warehouse demos (D5, D6) stacked in NOMAD.3dm. IFC: the same stacked prisms.
experiments.result: 4,823 buildings with no homes: 1,741 warehouses, 1,989 commercial, 1,093 office. Of those not in use by the census hint, 893 stand in a zone that admits housing (259 warehouses, 482 commercial, 152 office) and 403 in a zone whose own plan decides. On 40 empty warehouses in zones that admit housing (6 m clear height, mezzanine): 48 homes in 13 buildings, all passing Group B; patios used in 5. Most of the rest are small sheds and garages (50-300 m²). An empty 365 m² nau on Av. Marquès de Castellbell gets 8 homes on 2 levels.
learned: The mezzanine doubles the homes in a 6 m tall nau. The stair-and-lift core costs one flat's width per street door.
Deep halls behind a narrow street front stay empty: beyond 25 m from the only street door, CTE DB-SI SI 3 asks for a second exit, which NOMAD does not model yet.
Which buildings are really unused needs a better source than the ground-floor census.
experiments.decision: Keep: whole buildings as Group B, mezzanine for tall warehouses, patios only where they light homes, one core per street door. Next: a second exit for deep halls, a real vacancy source, and offices with their own storey heights.
figures: Warehouses, commercial and office buildings with no homes, by what their zone allows (left: all; right: not in use by the census hint).

Two empty warehouses with 6 m clear height, on two levels (mezzanine). Grey: stair and lift core; blue: a patio cut through. Bottom: the hall behind a narrow front stays empty (it would need a second exit).

experiments.title: A second street door for deep buildings; looking for vacancy and height data
experiments.question: Can the deep part of a building behind a patio get homes when it is more than 25 m from the main street door?
did: Fire escape (CTE DB-SI SI 3, checked in the rulebook): with one exit, every route is at most 25 m. With more than one exit it may reach 50 m, or 35 m where people sleep.

src/generate/building.py: when the part of a building behind a patio touches another street (a corner, or a building through the block), it gets its own street door on that street, and every home in it is measured to that door (25 m).

Looked for an official register of empty buildings and for building heights in Barcelona Open Data and at ICGC. None found. The 2024 census of ground-floor premises stays the vacancy hint, and the user sets the clear or storey height in step 2.
experiments.result: 67 of the 818 candidate buildings in zones that admit housing (not in use by the census hint) have a part behind a patio on a second street. In 12 tested, the second door adds homes in several: an 903 m² office building 44 -> 55 homes, a 1,073 m² office building 30 -> 40, a 504 m² commercial building 18 -> 24, a 453 m² office building 24 -> 32. The 40-warehouse sample is unchanged (48 homes): those naus have one street.
learned: A second street is the simplest legal second exit for a deep building.
Halls behind a single narrow street front still stay empty: they would need a second exit through a neighbour's plot or the block interior, which needs the neighbours' or the city's consent.
experiments.decision: Keep: a second street door wherever the deep part reaches another street. Vacancy and heights: ask the user (own list, height in step 2) until an official source exists.

experiments.title: The 29 October crits: real daylight, liveable zones, temporary homes, a city view, the metropolitan area, precedents
experiments.question: What did the three critics ask for that NOMAD still did not do, and can it do it now?
did: Real daylight in the check (critic B, 'people don't need to live in a jail'): the generator and the final check now use Bars's predicted lit depth for each shop (DF >= 2 %, E20), or 5,5 m labelled as an assumption where there is none. A living room or bedroom passes only with at least half its floor within that depth (NOMAD liveability, not law).
Liveable zones ('blue spots'): the website draws the floor in lit / service / dark bands in the first tile of every design ('As it is: where light reaches').

Temporary / emergency homes (critics A and C): read the law first. 'Allotjament temporal de protecció' is only allowed on public land for facilities (TRLU art. 34.5 quater), not in a private shop. The route that fits a shop is shared-space housing (Llei 18/2007 art. 3.p and 18 bis, DL 50/2020, DT 10a, Circular 8 AHC): a private space of at least 24 m² plus shared rooms of at least 6 m² per home (6 m², 2,45 m circle, lit). In Barcelona the private space plus its share of the shared rooms must reach 40 m² (MPGM 2004 DA1 2.a with art. 18 bis.2, the stricter reading). Density may be exceeded for homes for groups needing social attention (MPGM 2004 DA2). src/generate/shared.py: small studios, the best-lit ones become shared living rooms and kitchens until every home has its proportional share. Website: 'Kind of homes' in step 2.

For the city (critic A: policy makers): src/check/city_runs.py ran NOMAD on all 1,694 clean empty shops and all 1,206 warehouses, commercial and office buildings not in use by the census hint. Website section 'For the city': the homes the city needs, then the fewest places that reach it, by district, and what to avoid (not allowed, not liveable, keep it a shop, no legal home fits).

Beyond Barcelona (critic C): src/zoning/amb.py read the Catastro buildings of all 36 AMB towns (links from the Catastro's index) and their MUC zoning. Towns with their own plan are answered by the harmonised MUC code: A1 industrial, A2 tertiary and N non-urbanisable = no; R residential and other codes = the local plan decides.
Precedents (critic A): a website section with the sourced numbers (Barcelona, Madrid, Paris, England, APROP), each marked official or secondary.
experiments.result: Real daylight: on 40 real shops, 48 legal homes in 22 shops instead of 57 in 28; 9 homes in 6 shops had rooms mostly in the dark. City: 838 of 1,694 empty shops give 1,405 homes; unused buildings: 249 warehouses give 1,672 homes, 261 commercial buildings 3,414, 211 office buildings 8,077 (several storeys). In zones that admit housing: 6,442 homes; 1,000 homes need 13 places. Avoid: 1,159 not allowed, 949 not liveable, 464 keep it a shop, 739 where no legal home fits. AMB: 201,339 buildings; 15,885 warehouses, commercial and office buildings with no homes; 3,769 in a zone that admits housing, 2,177 where the local plan decides. Shared-space homes: in Barcelona's 40 m² rule they give as many homes as full flats (large demo shop: 6), smaller and with shared rooms.
learned: Real daylight removes about one home in six: the 5,5 m assumption was too kind.
Most homes in the city are in unused office buildings with several storeys, not in shops.
Shared-space housing is the legal small-home route for a shop, but Barcelona's 40 m² per home keeps it from adding homes; with the 36 m² of Decret 141/2012 it would.
experiments.decision: Keep: real daylight for every place with a prediction, the liveable zones on the plans, shared-space homes as a choice, the city view and the AMB layer. To confirm with the city: the 40 m² reading for shared-space homes and the density exception.
figures: The large demo shop: where light reaches (3 m lit depth), full flats, and shared-space homes (green = shared living rooms and kitchens).
The metropolitan area: warehouses, commercial and office buildings with no homes, by what their zone allows.

experiments.title: NOMAD's own plan AI: trained on 15,545 real flats, every plan checked
experiments.question: Can an AI trained on real plans draw flats that fit a shop better than stretching the few real plans that pass?
did: Datasets searched (docs/plan_datasets_2026-11-03.md): Finch's library is not public; free to use: Swiss Dwellings and ResPlan (CC BY 4.0); RPLAN and LIFULL only on request for research. MSD's server was unreachable, and MSD is made from Swiss Dwellings anyway.

Training set (src/ai/plan_data.py): the 15,545 squared real flats of the plan library and their mirrors, 29,930 pictures at 0,25 m a pixel; the condition is the flat's rectangle, its window sides, the entrance and the number of bedrooms; the answer is a room type for every pixel.
Model (src/ai/train_plan.py, our own code): a U-Net with 4,3 million weights, trained 40 epochs (about 1 h) on the laptop's RTX 3060. 5 % of the flats were kept aside, never seen in training.

Picture to plan (src/ai/generate_plans.py): small blobs join their neighbour, walls are snapped to the plan's main wall lines (straight, orthogonal walls), every wall pixel joins a room (no dead area), doors are added as people walk (through a hall first, never through a bathroom), windows on the lit sides. Then the same checks as every real plan: plan graph, doors, turning circles, widths, daylight side, furniture, a kitchen and a bathroom, no room with more than 8 corners.

AI library: 5,760 street-flat slots (one-sided and through flats, 4,5-12 m wide, 6-10 m deep, 0-3 bedrooms, 5 entrance positions); the plans that pass every check join the street library as 'NOMAD AI'.

Also fixed: plan3 now drops a plan before ranking it when it would fail the flat checks (useful area, daylight depth, window share), so a plan that cannot pass no longer takes a slot from one that can.
experiments.result: On the 1,496 held-out flats: 70 % of pixels right, mIoU 0,57; 4 % of the drawn plans pass every check with straight walls (23 % with stepped walls, which were rejected). AI library: 227 plans from 5,760 slots. 40 real shops with Bars's daylight: 48 legal homes in 22 shops before; 52 in 25 with the ranking fix; 57 in 28 with the AI plans (36 AI flats used); median floor left unused per shop 134 -> 127 -> 101 m².
learned: The AI fills gaps the real plans leave (sizes and entrance positions no real plan has), so more of each shop becomes homes.
Straight walls matter more than quantity: most raw AI pictures need cleaning, and only clean ones are kept.
Studios and 1-beds are few in the training data (3,500 of 29,930), and 2-3 bed one-sided flats few in the AI library; RPLAN or LIFULL would add many.
experiments.decision: Keep: AI plans in the library, marked 'NOMAD AI', only when they pass every check; the ranking fix for all plans. Next: request RPLAN / LIFULL, train longer, and a diffusion model for more variety.
figures: Training: pixels right and room overlap on flats the model never saw.
Plans drawn by the AI for a rectangle, façade and entrance, cleaned to straight walls, furnished and passing every check.
Real shops with AI flats among the real ones.
